## relay pool run 2026-08-12 (run relay-20260812-001727-5554 — harness safety classifier vs the mechanical hops)

- [ ] 🔴 **The harness SAFETY CLASSIFIER blocked 39 of 237 agents in one pool run — it is now a systematic tax on relay's mechanical hops, not a rare event, and its two most-blocked classes leave REAL damage: stranded leases and a stale RELAY_STATUS** <!-- id:83c2 -->
  - **Observed** (run `relay-20260812-001727-5554`, `--intensive --quota-7d 40`, 2026-08-12 00:17→02:05): `agents_done=198, agents_error=39`. Blocked by hop class: **`release:<repo>:claim` ×17**, **`write-relay-status` ×6**, **`inject-take` ×6**, **`provision:<repo>` ×1**, **`gaming-log` ×1**. The pool still reached a clean drain and pushed 15 checkpoints, so this fails SOFT — which is exactly why it went unnoticed until the failure block was read.
  - **Real damage, both verified by command after the run**: (1) **two leases were left held** — `it-infra` and `lodelore`, both stamped `runId=relay-20260812-001727-5554`, still in `claim.sh peek` after the pool exited, because their release hops were blocked. A stranded lease blocks the NEXT pool from working that repo until the mtime-TTL expires. Released by hand at review. (2) **`RELAY_STATUS.md`'s header says `last updated 2026-08-11T23:44:16Z` while the file mtime is 02:05** — six blocked `write-relay-status` hops means the operator-facing status is silently hours stale mid-run, and it is the ONE artifact an `--afk` operator reads.
  - **The classifier's reasoning is coherent but structurally mistaken, and the mistake is stable**: it judges each sub-agent prompt in isolation, so a `claim.sh release <repo> --run <id>` reads as *"releasing a lease on a repo never mentioned in this session, under a run id the agent invented"*. From inside one hop that is a fair description — the run id WAS minted by the front door, and the repo was chosen by discovery, neither of which is visible in the hop's own prompt. It is the same misfire class as `routed:a923`, where it called a real user injection *"fabricated"*. **Do not "fix" this by weakening the hops** — the classifier is catching a genuine shape (an agent releasing a lease it cannot prove it owns); the gap is that relay gives it no provenance to check.
  - **Fix directions, none chosen — this needs a design decision**: (a) make each hop **self-attesting** — carry the acquiring evidence into the release prompt (the acquire's own output / the claim file's `runId`) so ownership is checkable from inside the hop, which is the honest answer to the classifier's actual objection; (b) **stop dispatching pure-mechanical hops as agents at all** where the mechanical daemon can run them (id:65f9/[[sandbox-2ec4]] — a shell hop that never needed an LLM cannot be blocked by a classifier that reads prompts); (c) make a blocked hop **fail LOUDLY into `state.agentFailures`** (id:06a1/id:a104) rather than only into the Workflow notification block — this run's 8 recorded agent-failures did NOT include the 39 classifier blocks, so the two failure channels are still disjoint. **(c) is the cheapest and is a strict improvement regardless of (a)/(b)** — it converts an invisible tax into a counted one.
  - **Note the asymmetry worth preserving**: the ONE blocked `provision:` hop did NOT cause damage — `id:66d9`'s fail-closed gate turned it into a visible handback with no child dispatched. That is the template: a hop whose failure is *consumed* is safe to have blocked; a hop whose failure is *ignored* (release, status-write) is not. Relates `routed:a923`, `id:06a1`, `id:a104`, `id:65f9`, `id:5937` (the deny-tail probe: `permissionMode=auto` denies nothing, so this classifier is a DIFFERENT enforcement layer than the permission system and is not covered by that finding).

## relay pool run findings 2026-08-12 (run `relay-20260812-122721-23819`, `--intensive --quota-7d 45`)

- [ ] [ROUTINE] **`/relay reconcile` is structurally blind to conflict-handback branches — in BOTH `--all` and per-repo modes — so "0 parked orphans" reads as a false clean while real unmerged work sits on disk** — `relay-reconcile.sh` enumerates ONLY `refs/heads/relay/orphan/*` (`ORPHAN_NS="relay/orphan/"`, `:91`, used by the `--all` sweep at `:361`). A branch enters that namespace only when a run DIES and its worktree is PARKED (id:689c). But a child that hits a ROADMAP.md merge conflict, correctly runs `git merge --abort`, and hands back leaves its branch under the LIVE name `relay/<runId>-<verdict>-repo-N` with the worktree still registered — it is never parked, so reconcile cannot see it in either mode. Measured 2026-08-12 after run `relay-20260812-122721-23819`: `relay-reconcile.sh --all` reported `0 parked orphan(s) across all own repos` and the per-repo form reported `no parked orphans`, while FOUR branches held real unmerged commits (cartulary `execute-repo-1` 297890b, dotclaude-skills `review-repo-0` e28ecb1, escapement `review-repo-0` 931a908, loderite `review-repo-1` 3ad14ec). The handbacks DID name each worktree path, so the information exists in `RELAY_STATUS.md` — but the tool a human is told to run for exactly this ("recover via `/relay reconcile`") answers "nothing here". Note this is NOT a bug in `--all` (which is correctly scoped to parked orphans, id:4e14); the gap is that conflict-handback branches never join the class `--all` enumerates. Fix candidates: (a) have the integrator PARK a conflict-handback branch into `relay/orphan/*` on abort, so the existing consume path finds it — smallest change, reuses id:689c wholesale; (b) widen reconcile to also list live `relay/<runId>-*` branches whose run is no longer in `heartbeat.sh live-runs`, kept distinct from parked orphans in the output; (c) both. (a) is preferred — one namespace, one consume path. Until then a human must read `RELAY_STATUS.md` Blocked worktree paths, which is precisely the manual step reconcile exists to remove. <!-- id:2b4b -->

- [ ] [ROUTINE] **The `id:3801` auto hard-split files executable seams under a repo's parked heading, where every heading-aware reader correctly ignores them** — cartulary's `## Deferred (named reopen triggers — see CLAUDE.md §Scope)` heading held only rejected/deferred PROSE bullets (FUSE mount, custom merge driver, pre-receive hook — each with a named reopen trigger). The splitter appended three real, fully-specced `[HARD]` seams of `id:9c14` beneath it: `id:66de` (derive-step skeleton + A7 enforcement-config refusal), `id:3f96` (A4 repair entry point), `id:7139` (A5 merge-damage instrument) — each carrying Acceptance + Done-check + Context and pointing at concrete new files. `roadmap-lint.sh` has ALWAYS treated items under that heading as parked, and as of `id:4b8f` `gather-repo-state.sh` agrees, so cartulary's `open_hard_pool` went 4 → 1 and those three seams are now invisible to dispatch. **This is a filing bug, not a counter bug** — the counter now matches the ratified section semantics and the ROADMAP's own prose; the seams are simply in the wrong section. Two dispositions, and it is the OWNER'S call which: (a) MOVE the three seams up under `## Current` (they look genuinely executable — if so they should have been there all along, and the `4 → 1` is a real loss of dispatchable work); or (b) leave them parked because `id:9c14` is genuinely gated, in which case the splitter is correct-by-accident and the only fix is the ROADMAP prose. Either way the SPLITTER needs the durable fix: it must never append an executable seam under a heading its own repo treats as parked — check `is_exempt_heading` (now shared, `relay/scripts/lib-roadmap-sections.sh`) at the insertion point and refuse/relocate. Sibling of the already-filed splitter defects `id:7756` (mints seam ids by regexing a token out of the seam's own subject text) and `id:cd9c` — the same component, third distinct defect. **OWNER-DECIDED 2026-08-14 (`/relay human .`): BOTH halves — move the three seams under `## Current`, AND land the durable splitter fix.** The owner read the `4 → 1` as a REAL loss of dispatchable work: `id:66de`/`id:3f96`/`id:7139` each carry Acceptance + Done-check + Context and point at concrete new files, so they are genuinely executable and should have been under `## Current` all along. **This repo owns only the SPLITTER half** (the seams live in cartulary, another repo — not editable from here mid-flight, and a live pool may hold it): the splitter must check `is_exempt_heading` (shared, `relay/scripts/lib-roadmap-sections.sh`) at the INSERTION point and refuse or relocate, so it can never append an executable seam under a heading its own repo treats as parked. **Acceptance**: a fixture repo with a parked heading — the splitter must NOT insert an executable seam beneath it; assert the refuse/relocate path, not merely that the counter changed. The cartulary seam-move half is ROUTED to that repo via the shared inbox this pass. Sibling splitter defects in the same component: `id:7756`, `id:cd9c` — third distinct defect, worth asking whether the component needs a rewrite rather than a third patch. **OWNER-DECIDED 2026-08-14 (`/relay human .`): PATCH — add the `is_exempt_heading` check at the insertion point; no splitter rewrite** (same ruling as `id:7756`; a THIRD distinct defect in this component is the pre-registered trigger to revisit). **CORRECTION to this item's own closing sentence, verified this pass:** it calls `id:cd9c` a sibling *"splitter defect ... the same component, third distinct defect"*. Wrong — `id:cd9c` is a defect in **`roadmap-archive.sh`** (teach the generic archiver to leave a stub), a DIFFERENT script. The `id:3801` hard-split has **TWO** filed defects, not three: this one and `id:7756`. The miscount matters because it was the stated evidence for a rewrite. <!-- id:90d6 -->

## `/relay review` 2026-08-13 findings (window `relay-ckpt-20260812-1417..HEAD`, 13 commits)

- [ ] [ROUTINE] **`append.sh`'s one-entry-per-persona invariant (`id:069b`) holds only WITHIN one working tree — a `merge=union` merge breaks it and nothing reconciles the result.** `meeting/personas.md` is `merge=union` (confirmed via `git check-attr`). If two branches each extend the same persona, union merge keeps BOTH lines; a later extend then merges into the first only, leaving a duplicate `**Name**` line permanently plus intra-line duplication of the shared base text. `personas-conformance.sh` detects the duplicate-name state LOUDLY, so this fails visibly rather than silently — which is why it is a decision, not a bug: the options are (a) leave it, relying on the loud detector plus a human merge, (b) teach the extend path to reconcile duplicate `**Name**` lines when it finds them, or (c) drop `merge=union` for this file and accept real conflicts. **Note (b) interacts with `00b1`/`244f`** — reconciling duplicates means a read-modify-write across the whole file, which needs the single-lock fix first. The union bias itself is right and is not in question: for a registry file a duplicated phrase is cosmetic while a dropped one is unrecoverable. Surfaced by independent re-derivation during the 2026-08-13 `/relay review`. **OWNER-DECIDED 2026-08-14 (`/relay human .`): option (b) — teach the extend path to RECONCILE duplicate `**Name**` lines.** Fix it at the write path rather than living with a loud detector plus manual merges. Option (c), dropping `merge=union`, was rejected for the reason the item itself states: the union bias is correct for a registry file, since a duplicated phrase is cosmetic while a DROPPED persona line is unrecoverable, and a botched conflict resolution can drop one. **GATED, and the gate is load-bearing:** reconciling duplicates is a read-modify-write across the whole file, so it MUST NOT be built before the single-lock fix (`id:00b1`/`id:244f`) — building it first races exactly the concurrent writers it is meant to repair. **Acceptance**: two branches each extending the same persona, union-merged, then a third extend — the result has ONE `**Name**` line retaining BOTH branches' additions and no intra-line duplication of the shared base text; `personas-conformance.sh` clean. Never resolve a duplicate by DELETING one side. <!-- gated-on:00b1,244f --> <!-- id:8ed8 -->

## inbox intake 2026-08-13 — `/relay review` (dead-letter targeting this repo)

- [ ] [INPUT — decision] **Investigate overlayfs/fuse-overlayfs (or similar union mount) for per-agent / per-session repo views — SCOPED to artifact-provisioning + read-only enforcement, NOT as a worktree replacement.** Owner-raised 2026-08-21. IDEA: give each agent/session a copy-on-write union view over the canonical repo instead of (or alongside) a `git worktree`, so it sees the full tree in its own context and writes land in an upper layer. **WHERE IT GENUINELY WINS (2 dimensions, both real today):** (1) it DISSOLVES `id:34b7` part (2) — `provision-worktree.sh` exists only because a fresh worktree lacks the GITIGNORED build artifacts (`node_modules`, `.venv`, caches), so the parent symlinks them "best-effort" and its own header admits it is "deliberately NOT exhaustive"; loderite `RELAY_LOG.md:2681` (with `:3022/:3422/:3486`) shows children then REMOVING those symlinks again before commit. An overlay gives the complete tree for free, exhaustively, with COW writes — the provisioning step and the symlink-removal dance both disappear. (2) mounting the lower layer READ-ONLY is OS-level ENFORCEMENT of a read-only/pure-agent contract rather than a documented promise (the enforce-don't-document principle; relates the `id:23ab` formal-enforcement frontier). **WHERE IT DOES NOT HELP — record this so it is not re-litigated:** it does NOT address merge/semantic reconciliation, which is the actual bottleneck when several agents work one repo. Two agents editing the same file in two overlays conflict at merge exactly as in two worktrees; worktrees yield branches + real commits + `git merge`, an overlay yields a filesystem delta with NO history. Overlays improve the already-solved half (concurrent working state) and leave the hard half untouched. **BLOCKERS to settle BEFORE any build:** (a) the appealing property — SAME PATH, different content per agent — requires a per-agent MOUNT NAMESPACE (`unshare -m`); two processes cannot see different content at one path otherwise, and Claude Code's Bash tool does not launch agents in separate mount namespaces, so this needs harness support that does not exist today. Without it the overlay sits at a different path = a worktree with worse git integration, i.e. the idea loses its whole point. (b) `.git` semantics — if `.git` is inside the overlay, commits land in the UPPER layer's object store and are invisible to the canonical repo until `git fetch <overlaypath>`, which is worktrees-with-extra-steps; if `.git` is bind-mounted read-only the agent cannot commit at all. (c) privileges — overlayfs mount traditionally needs `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`; unprivileged overlay in a user namespace works on modern kernels (zomni is 6.18) and `fuse-overlayfs` is the rootless fallback, but that is a new dependency and a new failure mode. **RECOMMENDED SHAPE IF PURSUED:** do NOT frame it as replacing worktrees. Frame it as "overlay-provisioned worktree" — keep the git worktree for branch/commit/merge semantics, and use a union mount only to supply the gitignored artifact layer, which is (1) above and needs no mount namespace. That variant is buildable today and dissolves `id:34b7` part (2) outright. The full same-path per-agent view stays gated on harness mount-namespace support. Related: `id:34b7`, `id:c6c8` (Agent-tool `isolation: worktree` is CWD-repo-relative), `id:3558`, `id:23ab`. <!-- id:458c -->
- [ ] [INPUT — decision] **Whitelist the destructive-git ops in a PROVABLY-DISPOSABLE context — the deny-always ruling is right for the canonical repo and wrong for a throwaway worktree/overlay.** Owner-raised 2026-08-22, alongside the ruling that `reset --hard`/`checkout -- .`/`restore .`/`clean -f`/`stash drop` become UNCONDITIONAL deny for Claude's Bash tool. **THE MOTIVATING CASE IS THE ONE THAT JUST FIRED:** the review agent's `git reset --hard` was refused, but it was running inside `.claude/worktrees/agent-a91eea216b1222d09` — a disposable, agent-owned linked worktree. A reset there destroys nothing the owner cares about; the parent had explicitly asked it to mutate-and-restore a file, so the NEED was legitimate and only the TOOL was wrong. Deny-always therefore forbids a safe operation in the one context where agents most need it, which will push agents toward worse workarounds (hand-rolled `cp` backups, `python3` rewrites — the very read-modify-write pattern CLAUDE.md bans). **THE HARD PART IS "PROVABLY":** the guard must PROVE disposability itself, never take the caller's word, and must FAIL CLOSED on any doubt — a wrong "isolated" verdict silently reopens the exact hole the ruling closes. Candidate proofs, all cheap and checkable inside a PreToolUse hook: cwd resolves under `.claude/worktrees/` (or `~/.cache/relay/worktrees/`); `git rev-parse --git-dir` differs from `--git-common-dir` (i.e. a LINKED worktree, not the main checkout); HEAD is on a throwaway branch (`worktree-agent-*`, `relay/*`) rather than a trunk; the path is not the repo root of any `relay.toml` own-repo. Require ALL of them, not any. Note the guard sees only the COMMAND STRING and the tool payload — it must derive cwd itself and cope with `git -C <path>` and a `cd X && git …` prefix pointing somewhere else entirely; a naive cwd check is defeated by `git -C ~/src/<repo> reset --hard` issued FROM a worktree. **STRONGER PRIMITIVE, ALREADY FILED:** `id:458c` (overlayfs/fuse-overlayfs or mount namespaces per agent) would make this decidable rather than heuristic — in a namespace where the canonical tree is not even visible, or is a read-only lower layer, a destructive command CANNOT reach it and the guard question dissolves instead of being adjudicated. That is the "prefer dissolving a problem structurally over guarding it" heuristic, and it is a genuine argument FOR the overlay work that `id:458c` currently lacks (its recorded wins are artifact-provisioning and read-only enforcement; this is a third). **DO NOT BUILD THE WHITELIST BEFORE THE DENY** — ship the unconditional deny first (it is the safe direction), then relax it only for a context the guard can prove. Relates `id:3a09`, `id:458c`, `id:9320` (destructive-op containment, `[INPUT — meeting]`), and `id:5937` (auto mode denies nothing across the 12 probed classes — OS/hook containment is the only real boundary). — **OWNER REFINEMENT 2026-08-22: the five guarded ops are NOT one blast-radius class; the worktree whitelist is well-founded for three and WEAKEST for `clean -f/-d`.** Owner's observation, and it is correct: `checkout -- .` / `restore .` "can't kill anything not already committed or yet untracked" — they discard uncommitted modifications to TRACKED files only; committed work survives in git and UNTRACKED files are untouched. The hard-reset form is the same plus a possible HEAD move, and commits orphaned that way ARE reflog-recoverable. So for those three the blast radius is exactly "uncommitted tracked edits in THIS checkout", which under worktree-per-agent is the agent's OWN work — the guard's stated rationale ("including a parallel session's or a human's in-flight edits") is precisely the part worktree isolation dissolves. **THE EXCEPTION INVERTS THE MODEL: `clean -f/-d` destroys UNTRACKED files** — the exact category the other three leave alone. No reflog, no stash, no recovery of any kind. In an agent worktree the untracked set includes the `id:34b7` provisioned gitignored artifacts and any scratch file that is the only copy of something. So a worktree-scoped exemption is well-founded for checkout/restore/hard-reset, THIN for `stash drop|clear` (the entry survives only in an unreferenced reflog either way), and should probably NOT extend to `clean` at all.

   | op | kills | survives |
   |---|---|---|
   | `checkout -- .` / `restore .` | uncommitted TRACKED edits | committed, untracked |
   | hard reset | same, plus HEAD move (orphans are reflog-recoverable) | committed, untracked |
   | `clean -f/-d` | UNTRACKED files | committed, tracked edits |
   | `stash drop\|clear` | stash entries (unreferenced reflog only) | working tree |

   **THIRD INDEPENDENT ARGUMENT FOR SANDBOXING (owner-raised):** the residual cross-session hazard after worktrees is an agent that `cd`s into ANOTHER repo — which no command-string guard can reliably catch, since `git -C <path>` and a `cd X && …` prefix both defeat a cwd check. OS-level containment (relay subusers, the `id:8e7a`/`id:5bef` cluster) or a mount namespace (`id:458c`) makes that structurally impossible rather than adjudicated. A third recorded win for that work, alongside artifact-provisioning and read-only enforcement. — **OWNER PROPOSAL 2026-08-22, the concrete FIRST SLICE: RE-PERMIT `restore .` and `checkout -- .` (only those two) when the command has no cross-repo redirect AND the cwd is a provably disposable worktree.** Owner's wording: *"I just suggested re-permitting restore/checkout (without `-C <other-repo>`)"* — note this RELAXES the unconditional deny for the two mildest ops; it is not a further tightening, and the parent initially mis-read it as one. **WHY THESE TWO FIRST:** their blast radius is uncommitted TRACKED edits in one checkout — committed work survives in git, untracked files are untouched — so under worktree-per-agent it is the agent's OWN work, which is self-limiting. They are also the ops the guard's own refusal text recommends as remedy #2 in scoped form, so a blanket deny leaves agents nothing but hand-rolled `cp`/Python read-modify-write, which CLAUDE.md bans and which ALSO bypasses the flock on shared ledgers. **THE MACHINERY ALREADY EXISTS — this is not greenfield:** `hooks/destructive-git-guard.py:179` defines `_GIT_GLOBAL_WITH_VALUE = {"-C","--git-dir","--work-tree","-c","--exec-path","--namespace"}` and `classify_git_argv()` (`:356`) tokenises argv, so a command that redirects at another tree IS detectable. Required conjunction, ALL of them, fail-closed on any doubt: (1) tokenisation succeeded — if `_UNPARSEABLE_CONSTRUCT` (`:176`: `$(`, backtick, `<<`, `<(`) forced the raw fallback, DENY, because the target cannot be established; (2) no `-C`/`--git-dir`/`--work-tree` argument present; (3) no `cd`/`pushd` prefix in the command; (4) cwd resolves under `.claude/worktrees/` or `~/.cache/relay/worktrees/`; (5) `git rev-parse --git-dir` differs from `--git-common-dir` (a LINKED worktree, not a main checkout); (6) HEAD is on a throwaway branch (`worktree-agent-*`, `relay/*`). **THE GAP THAT MUST NOT BE GLOSSED: the ORCHESTRATOR session has no worktree** — it works in the MAIN checkout, where uncommitted ledger edits sit routinely (they did repeatedly on 2026-08-22). "Worktrees eliminate the cross-session risk" is true of SUBAGENTS only, so condition (4)/(5) is what actually carries the safety, not the general adoption of worktrees. **EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE for this slice:** `clean -f/-d` (it destroys UNTRACKED files — the inverse blast radius, and in an agent worktree the untracked set includes the `id:34b7` provisioned artifacts), `stash drop|clear`, the hard-reset form, and all five force-push variants. Widen only on separate evidence. **ACCEPTANCE:** a scoped-path revert stays permitted everywhere (unchanged); the two whole-tree forms are permitted in a linked agent worktree and DENIED in the main checkout; a `-C <other-repo>` or `cd <other-repo> &&` variant is DENIED wherever it is issued; an unparseable command is DENIED. Test the DENY side first — a permissive bug here is silent. <!-- id:6a6b -->
- [ ] [ROUTINE] **The destructive-git guard FALSE-POSITIVES on documentation — writing PROSE about a guarded command is refused as if executing it.** Hit live 2026-08-22, minutes after the guard went unconditional: appending a TODO item that described the guarded operations was refused, because the ledger text was carried inside a Bash heredoc and the guard's raw scan matched the command string in the prose. The write was documentation, not execution. **THIS IS THE COST OF A DELIBERATE DESIGN CHOICE, not a simple bug** — the raw scan exists precisely so a command hidden in a quoted string (`bash -c "…"`, an `eval`, a generated script) cannot evade the guard, so "ignore occurrences inside strings" would open exactly the evasion hole the raw scan closes. Parsing harder is not obviously the answer either: the guard sees only a command string, and distinguishing "a heredoc whose BODY is data" from "a heredoc whose body is piped to a shell" is the halting-problem end of shell parsing. **KNOWN WORKAROUND, and it should be documented where agents will find it:** put the prose in a FILE via the `Write` tool and pass only the PATH on the command line (`jq -n --rawfile a <path> … | md-merge.py`), so the guarded string never enters a Bash command. That is already this repo's convention for other reasons (the `meeting/md-merge.py` flock'd path), so the fix may be purely documentary — say so in `hooks/README.md` and in the guard's own refusal text, which currently offers three remedies, none of which is "you were only writing about it". **WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE BLOCKED WRITE:** an agent that hits this without knowing the workaround sees an unexplained refusal on a legitimate ledger append, and the likely improvisations are exactly the banned ones — a Python read-modify-write, or `sed -i` — which bypass the flock as well. A guard whose false positives push agents toward `sed -i` on a shared ledger has traded one hazard for a worse one. Relates `id:3a09`, `id:6a6b`, and the `id:6059` marker-ambiguity guard, which solved the analogous "text ABOUT a marker vs text CARRYING a marker" problem by refusing loudly and telling the author to de-literalise — the same shape of answer may fit here. — **NARROWED 2026-08-22 after reading the guard: the false positive is NOT "prose vs execution", it is "HEREDOCS DISABLE TOKENISATION".** `hooks/destructive-git-guard.py:176` defines `_UNPARSEABLE_CONSTRUCT = re.compile(r"\$\(|`|<<|<\(")`; the raw-text patterns at `:183+` are used ONLY when tokenisation is impossible, and their own comment says they are "deliberately narrow: they must not fire on a path-scoped revert mentioned inside a commit message". So the guard ALREADY tries not to match prose — what defeated it was the `<<` in a Bash heredoc, which forced the raw fallback, after which the prose matched. **That makes the fix much smaller than this item first claimed:** it is not "teach a hook to distinguish documentation from execution" (which is the halting-problem end of shell parsing), it is "a heredoc whose body is DATA, not a command, currently forces the conservative fallback". Options worth weighing, none obviously right: recognise the specific `cmd <<'EOF' … EOF` data-heredoc shape (careful — `bash <<'EOF'` IS execution); or leave the behaviour and simply DOCUMENT the workaround in the refusal text, which currently lists three remedies and not the one that applies ("you were only writing about it — put the text in a file via the Write tool and pass the PATH"). The Write-tool route is already this repo's convention for ledger appends, so documenting may be the whole fix. Correction recorded because the original framing would have sent someone at a far harder problem than the real one. **RECURRED 2026-08-22 (`/relay human`), and this time it BLOCKED ledger work rather than merely annoying a doc write — third confirmed instance.** While filing the owner's tier-(b) decisions, a `md-merge.py` payload was built in a heredoc; the payload's PROSE quoted the guarded tree-wide reset form (it was describing the very bypass `id:fb2c` is about), and the guard refused the whole Bash call. The refusal text was correct on its own terms and the fallback was cheap (build the JSON payload with the Write tool instead, so no destructive string ever reaches Bash), but note the shape: **the guard's false positive fired on the pass whose job was to document the guard.** This is direct evidence for the narrowed diagnosis already recorded here — heredocs (`<<`) disable tokenisation, and ONLY then does the raw-pattern fallback match prose — and it pins a concrete, recurring cost: any ledger write whose text quotes a guarded command must route around Bash. Related: `id:fb2c` (the wrapper-scan fix) carries a cross-note, since widening `_RAW_PATTERNS` to `eval`/`bash -c`/`sh -c` payloads WITHOUT fixing this class would widen the false-positive surface at the same time — sequence the two deliberately. <!-- id:9979 -->

MEASURED footprint (chars/4): `relay-loop.js` **77,400 tok**; next largest `integrate.sh` 12,883; `run-anomaly-scan.sh` 7,339; a whole-item `grep id:4d44 TODO.md` 4,401. So the ledgers did NOT cause those overflows — this file did. A Sonnet agent whose brief spans this file plus two others cannot hold it; the agent with a bounded file set (one 3,812-tok hook + its test) completed normally. **THE BLOCKER — do not scope this without settling it:** the Workflow sandbox **cannot `import`**. Three files say so in their own headers — `pool-args.mjs:7` ("Workflow sandbox cannot `import`, so relay-loop.js carries BYTE-IDENTICAL inline copies"), `handback-guard.mjs:12`, `redispatch-guard.mjs:8`. That is WHY the file is monolithic. The existing extract-to-`.mjs`-and-pin-with-a-structural-test pattern buys TESTABILITY, not size: the inline duplicate remains, so `relay-loop.js` does not shrink by one byte. Therefore the only real modularization is a **BUILD/BUNDLE STEP** that assembles `relay-loop.js` from modules before dispatch — and `CLAUDE.md:29` states *"There is no build step, no version manifest, and no release process — the live install IS the published version"*. That is an owner-level architecture decision, not a refactor. **SECOND BLOCKER:** an owner **do-not-modify directive on `relay-loop.js` (`id:4313`)** exists and had to be explicitly scope-lifted in a meeting for even the small `id:6217` extraction — so any work here needs that lift first. **COSTS OF THE STATUS QUO, measured today:** two agent losses (~300k tokens of abandoned work, recovered only by manual salvage); every brief touching the relay loop must be Opus-tier or carry explicit slicing discipline; `documentSymbol` over it returns 53 KB. **IF PURSUED**, the honest options are (a) a bundle step (breaks the no-build-step convention — decide that first), (b) shrink by DELETING rather than moving: the drain-path duplication is already recorded moot-by-retirement (`id:7488`), and `drain-driver.mjs` is frozen, so some inline copies may have no live consumer — audit before assuming, (c) accept the size and mandate slicing discipline in every brief (cheapest, fixes nothing structurally). - [ ] [INPUT — decision] **Delegated Sonnet agents die at ~175k tokens, and ~34% of that window is spent BEFORE the first tool call — measured from seven real transcripts, 2026-08-21.** THREE Sonnet subagents died `Prompt is too long` in one session; a Sonnet control and three full-tier controls survived. Diagnosed by a dedicated agent parsing the JSONL transcripts (deliberately delegated so the bulk never entered the parent's context — that method worked and is worth reusing). **NUMBERS (from API `usage`, authoritative):** effective ceiling **~175k**, not 200k — last successful requests 172,450 / 171,959 / 174,207, consistent with a 200k budget minus a ~24k `max_tokens` output reserve. A full-tier control ran **200,534 input tokens and SUCCEEDED**, so full-tier subagents are not on a 200k window (they inherit the parent's 1M model). **BASELINE PREAMBLE = 58.6k tokens before the first tool call** (system prompt + CLAUDE.md + memory index + tool definitions) — 34% of the usable window, the single largest line item and the only one that is free to cut. **TWO REFUTED HYPOTHESES, both stated confidently by the parent before measuring:** (1) "big-file reads caused it, slicing discipline fixes it" — the agent that OBEYED the discipline (19 bounded `sed -n`/`grep` slices, never a whole-file read) spent 48,793 chars on the same file family versus 50,345 for the undisciplined one, and died at the HIGHEST peak of the three. Discipline changed the SHAPE (19 small slices vs 4 big) not the VOLUME, and each extra slice bought another full thinking turn. No casualty ever read `relay-loop.js` whole. (2) "narrow the brief and Sonnet is fine" — the narrowest brief (2 files, ~12k tok, explicit discipline) still died. **ACTUAL CAUSE — baseline + ACCUMULATION, dominated by the agent's OWN OUTPUT:** for the crux case the agent's cumulative `output_tokens` was **50,607 vs ~33k of tool results** — extended thinking, not reading. Growth was strictly monotonic, no single result above 13.3k tokens. The SURVIVOR made MORE tool calls (86 vs 27/53/42) with a mean result of 1,130 chars (vs 7,112/2,656/3,148), and is the ONLY transcript showing a **microcompaction** (141,876 → 133,256) — the casualties never received one. **CONCRETELY PREVENTIVE, in order of leverage:** (a) **shrink the delegated-agent preamble** — 58.6k is the biggest and cheapest lever, and it is fleet-wide, not repo-specific; does a subagent need the full memory index and every tool definition? (b) scope briefs so no in-scope file exceeds ~15k chars, and PRE-EXTRACT the relevant TODO item text into the brief instead of having the agent grep a 927 KB ledger; (c) route WRITE-HEAVY work (many Edit/Write turns, which drove the two worst output totals) to full tier, where 200k+ demonstrably passes; (d) cap `Read`/`grep` output at the TOOL layer rather than by instruction — instruction-level discipline is now empirically shown not to work. NOTE (c) is a cost decision: full tier per delegated implementation task vs. losing ~130-200k tokens of uncommitted work per casualty (three times today; all three had to be salvaged and committed by hand because agents that die never commit). Related `id:9397` (relay-loop.js size — a real but SECONDARY factor), `id:b59f` (LSP). **RE-MEASURED 2026-08-22 ON A LIVE POOL RUN — the tax is WORSE than the 2026-08-21 figure, and it is UNIFORM ACROSS TIERS.** Source: run `relay-20260822-102233-32252`, per-agent first-message input (input + cache_read + cache_creation) from the workflow's agent transcripts. **Median first prompt, before any tool call: Opus 64,880 · Sonnet 66,580 · Haiku 48,118.** The 2026-08-21 estimate was 58.6k; the measured figure is ~65k. **The uniformity is the finding:** Opus and Sonnet pay essentially the same preamble, so this is NOT model behaviour — it is the harness system prompt plus tool definitions, which is exactly what a custom agent definition replaces. Per-agent peaks in that run: Sonnet 87,129 / 92,362 / 113,793 (n=3); Opus up to 158,847 (n=6). **So for the three Sonnet agents, preamble was 59-77% of their ENTIRE context footprint**, and across the run's ten real agents (103 of the 114 were `model:"bash"` mechanical hops with a 1-token prompt) that is roughly **650k tokens of pure preamble in a single run**. - [ ] [HARD] **RE-VERIFY the prompt-size gate's PREMISE against real transcripts — it was built on an unmeasured causal story, and today's measurement does not match it.** Owner-raised 2026-08-21: *"I assume no pool run with the prompt too long ever investigated the actual transcripts, so much of our work on TODO/ROADMAP slicing might have been in vain."* The gate (`id:4f9b`/`id:b018`/`id:35b7`) estimates an assembled child prompt from LEDGER BYTES and refuses dispatch above a 100k budget — its handback literally reads *"the assembled execute prompt … is ~315,704 tok … CAUSE: ROADMAP.md is too large … TODO.md is too large"*. **Two things now need checking, and NEITHER is settled by today's data:** (1) **Are those bytes actually IN the child's prompt?** `unitPrompt()` INSTRUCTS the child to read ledgers; it does not embed them. If they enter as TOOL RESULTS mid-run rather than as prompt text, the gate is estimating the wrong quantity — the concern stays real (reading a 927 KB TODO.md ≈ 231k tok would certainly kill a child) but the ESTIMATE, the threshold, and the framing are miscalibrated. (2) **The threshold should be re-derived from measured numbers**: baseline 58.6k + a ~175k ceiling leaves ~116k of working room for a Sonnet child, against a 100k budget picked without measurement. **DO NOT conclude the slicing work was wasted** — `id:e68f`'s slice measured 3,854 B vs 1,157,395 B, and casualties' cumulative tool results ran 33-48k tokens, so not reading the ledgers is genuinely worth a third of the window. What is unverified is the CAUSAL STORY the gate encodes, and that story is what future work will be built on. METHOD: the transcripts of pool children that died `Prompt is too long` are the evidence; delegate the parse (see the sibling item) so the bulk never enters the analysing context — that method worked today. Related `id:10dc`, `id:e68f`, `id:4f9b`, `id:b018`, `id:35b7`, and the D2-A "bytes actually READ per dispatched item" metric, which is the right measurement and is still unbuilt. — **CORRECTION 2026-08-22, this item was FILED ON A FALSE PREMISE.** It says the gate's causal story "was never checked". **It WAS checked, and the answer is already recorded in `ROADMAP.md`** under the `id:4f9b`/`id:93cc` cluster: a real pool child died `Prompt is too long` while `roadmap_bytes` was 254,087 (~63.5k tok), so the gate's estimate landed near 77k against its 100k cap and it **correctly did NOT fire** — the child then created its worktree and produced **566 committed lines** (`lint-embedded-literals.mjs` + test, `id:ef9e`) BEFORE dying. Recorded verdict: *"the death was in-session context growth, not prompt assembly"*, with `id:4f9b` closing the **dispatch-time** half and the **run-time** half left uncovered. Today's `id:10dc` transcript measurement reached the SAME conclusion independently, from a different dispatch path (parent-session `Agent` subagents, not pool children): baseline 58.6k + accumulation + the agent's own output, not prompt assembly. **TWO independent investigations, one answer — so there is nothing left to investigate.** The owner's framing ("might have been in vain, nobody checked") and this item's original framing were both wrong in the same direction; the real situation is worse in one respect and better in another: the finding EXISTS and has simply not been acted on. **WHAT ACTUALLY REMAINS — split by who can decide it.** MECHANICAL (delegable): (a) re-derive the 100k threshold from measured numbers — ~175k ceiling minus the 58.6k preamble ≈ **~116k working room** for a Sonnet child, versus a 100k cap chosen without measurement; (b) build the **death-cause record** the ROADMAP item calls load-bearing, so a dispatch-time death and a run-time death stop being indistinguishable in the ledger — that indistinguishability is the stated reason the wrong remedy keeps getting recommended. OWNER'S CALL (do NOT delegate): (c) `relay/scripts/prompt-size-gate.mjs:72` prescribes `roadmap-archive.sh` as THE remedy, which is wrong for a run-time death AND — per the adjacent ROADMAP note — barely shrinks the live file any more, since one stub line accrues per archived item permanently. Changing it means changing what a **fail-closed dispatch gate** does: loosen it wrongly and doomed children dispatch, tighten it wrongly and healthy repos starve (the `id:e7e4` failure mode, live today). **STANDING CORRECTION for this fleet:** before filing "X was never verified", grep the ledger for X — this item cost a round-trip because the parent asserted an absence it had not checked, which is the same verify-before-asserting failure it was filed to describe. — **OWNER-DECIDED 2026-08-22 on (c): REMEDY TEXT ONLY; the 100k cap is UNCHANGED.** Fix what the gate RECOMMENDS — name the `id:e68f` slice and item-splitting as the real levers, demote `roadmap-archive.sh` to the conditional case it actually covers (only helps when the bulk is CLOSED; on this repo `TODO.md` is 95.6% OPEN, so it moves nothing), and state explicitly that a RUN-TIME death needs a different fix than a dispatch-time refusal. **The cap stays at 100k deliberately, NOT by omission.** Rationale, recorded so it is not "corrected" later by someone reading only the arithmetic: the derived ~116k working budget (~175k ceiling − 58.6k preamble) is real, but raising the cap toward it while the RUN-TIME half is still uncovered converts a LOUD, SAFE refusal (nothing dispatched, nothing lost, the repo surfaced in `RELAY_STATUS.md`) into a SILENT MID-WORK DEATH — and a dead child never commits: three on 2026-08-21 each stranded 130-200k tokens of finished work, recovered only because a human went looking in their worktrees. More dispatches that die is not an improvement over fewer that refuse. Revisit the cap only once run-time protection exists AND the death-cause record has produced real frequencies for each class. Pairs with the death-cause record now in build, which is what makes the two classes distinguishable at all — the ROADMAP item's own stated reason this was load-bearing. — **⚠ COMPOSE TRAP, measured 2026-08-22 — TWO independently wrong constants currently cancel out; fixing EITHER ALONE makes the gate WORSE.** `FIXED_OVERHEAD_TOKENS` is **12,000** against a MEASURED preamble of **58,600** (4.9× low), and `DISPATCH_TOKEN_BUDGET` is **100,000** against a DERIVED working budget of **116,400** (175,000 ceiling − 58,600 preamble). Real payload allowance today = 100,000 − 12,000 = **88,000 tok**, i.e. ~28,400 below the derived budget — approximately right by accident. **Correcting the overhead constant alone would tighten the gate by ~46,600 tok and refuse units that dispatch safely today.** They must move together or not at all; that is a second, independent reason the `id:299c`(c) ruling left BOTH untouched, beyond the loud-refusal-vs-silent-death argument. **ALSO VERIFIED AGAINST CODE (not inferred):** `unitPrompt()` (`relay-loop.js` ~2784) interpolates instructions, worktree/branch paths, `unit.reason` and the return schema and **embeds ZERO ledger bytes** — the ledgers reach a child as TOOL RESULTS if and when it reads them. So `roadmap_bytes`/`todo_bytes` are a dispatch-time FORECAST of run-time consumption, not a measurement of the assembled prompt: the number compared to the cap and the number that kills children are different quantities, and only the second is causal. This closes the open question in this item's original text. **RESIDUAL, needs an owner of BOTH files:** ruling items 1+2 (name the `id:e68f` slice first, demote archiving to the bulk-is-CLOSED case) were ALREADY in the emitted remedy — landed by `id:35b7`, asserted at `tests/test_prompt_size_gate_slice_35b7.sh:130-133`. What is genuinely missing is narrower: the unsliced branch's closing clause still says "splitting the ledger or pruning stale open items" rather than splitting the dispatched ITEM, and ruling item 3 (a run-time death needs a different fix from a dispatch-time refusal) appears in NO emitted string. Both are blocked because `oversizeDispatchReason`/`countedLedgersFor` are pinned BYTE-IDENTICAL to inline copies in `relay-loop.js` (`tests/test_prompt_size_gate_{4f9b,review_7c5f}.sh` extract the bodies and require verbatim substring matches), and `sliceInstruction` has an unpinned-but-real inline copy at `relay-loop.js:2666` that would silently diverge. All of it is recorded in the ~90-line provenance-marked comment block now in `prompt-size-gate.mjs`. <!-- id:299c -->
- [ ] [ROUTINE] **Capture every `Prompt is too long` failure durably and auto-dispatch a transcript analysis — today three agents died and their evidence survived only by luck.** Owner-raised 2026-08-21. The JSONL transcripts sit under a SESSION-SCOPED `/tmp` path (`/tmp/claude-*/…/tasks/<agentId>.output`) that does not survive a reboot or `/tmp` cleanup, and nothing flags the failure class at all — the parent only learns of it from a task-notification it may not act on. Three casualties today lost 130-200k tokens of finished-but-uncommitted work each, recovered ONLY because someone went looking in the worktrees. BUILD: (1) detect the failure class (the task-notification carries `Agent terminated early due to an API error: Prompt is too long`); (2) copy that agent's transcript to a durable location under `~/.claude/logs/` or `~/.config/relay/` before `/tmp` can lose it, with the brief, model tier, and file-set recorded alongside; (3) auto-dispatch the analysis to a DEDICATED agent that reports numbers only and never pastes transcript content back — the pattern that produced `id:10dc` (`~86k` subagent tokens, ~500 KB of JSONL kept entirely out of the parent's context); (4) also salvage-commit any uncommitted work in the dead agent's worktree, since agents that die never commit and this had to be done by hand three times today. Contract: after a `Prompt is too long` death, the transcript is durable, the work is committed as explicit WIP, and a numbers-only analysis exists without anyone having to think of asking. Related `id:10dc`, `id:4347` (a detector nobody invokes is a detector that reports on the schedule of someone remembering it). <!-- id:7b73 -->
- [ ] [ROUTINE] **Nothing in this fleet's tool-choice guidance mentions LSP — sessions and delegated agents navigate large files with whole-file `Read` when `goToDefinition`/`findReferences`/`hover` would answer the same question for a fraction of the context.** Owner-raised 2026-08-21. VERIFIED live: the LSP tool responds for this repo (a `documentSymbol` call on `relay-loop.js` returned a full symbol index; the TypeScript server and Pyright are both evidently running, since this session received unsolicited `typescript` diagnostics for `relay-loop.js` and Pyright diagnostics for `leAIrn2learn`). The global `CLAUDE.md` **"Tool choice for file edits"** section is detailed about Bash-vs-`Edit`-vs-`Read` — including that targeted `sed -n`/`grep` reads are ~40% cheaper than whole-file `Read`, "the fleet's second-largest context consumer" — and says **nothing at all about LSP**. So the cheapest navigation primitive available is absent from the very guidance written to control context cost. **CAVEAT, measured, do not overclaim:** `documentSymbol` is NOT automatically the win — on `relay-loop.js` it returned **53 KB** because it enumerates every local variable, versus ~310 KB for the whole file: ~6× better, still heavy. The genuine wins are the TARGETED operations — `findReferences` to answer "who calls this" without reading the file, `goToDefinition` to jump to one hunk, `hover` for a signature. **WHAT TO DO:** (1) benchmark the targeted ops against the equivalent `grep`/`Read` on a real question from today (e.g. "where is `parseIntegrateResult` consumed") and record actual numbers — this fleet's rule is that a mechanization claim needs a measurement, not a plausible story; (2) if they win, add an LSP paragraph to the tool-choice guidance and to the delegated-agent brief template, scoped to what actually helps rather than a blanket "prefer LSP"; (3) note the limits honestly — LSP needs a configured server per language, this repo is mostly **bash** (where LSP support is weak or absent), and the two files that hurt most today were `.js` (server available) and `.sh` (probably not). A rule that only helps the JS file should say so. Related: the `relay-loop.js` size item filed alongside this one, and the global CLAUDE.md tool-choice section. <!-- id:b59f -->
- [ ] [ROUTINE] **Install-drift keeps recurring and is only ever caught by a human reading a review — decide the gate.** `make install` publishes this repo via per-file symlinks, so a script added to a Makefile `*_FILES` list but never re-installed is invisible to every session that resolves it through `~/.claude/skills/`. Observed twice: the 2026-08-11 apex review found **5** un-symlinked relay scripts, and the 2026-08-12 review found `relay/scripts/mech-currency.sh` (resolved out-of-band by a `make install-relay` at 12. Aug 17:14 — `check-install-drift.sh` now reports the relay tree fully mirrored). **The detector already exists and is not wired to anything that fires**: `relay/scripts/check-install-drift.sh --canonical <dir> --installed <dir>` returns a clean verdict today, but nothing runs it automatically, so both occurrences were found by a human reading prose. That is the `id:4347` shape — a correct detector whose invocation is manual is a detector that reports on the schedule of someone remembering it. **The standing question, carried over from the 2026-08-12 review's REVIEW_ME box and rescued before that branch was disposed:** gate `make install` after a manifest touch (a pre-commit or post-checkout hook on `Makefile` `*_FILES` changes), or promote `relay-doctor`'s install-check to `--strict` on some path, or run `check-install-drift.sh` from a timer. Each has a different failure mode — a commit-time gate cannot see other machines, a `--strict` relay-doctor only fires when a relay runs, a timer needs a reporting channel that is not a log nobody reads. Owner's call on which, since it is a workflow-shape decision. Note this is the SECOND recurrence, so the observe-before-preventing threshold is met. Origin: the un-salvaged box on `relay/relay-20260812-122721-23819-review-repo-0`, whose *finding* was stale by disposal time but whose *question* was not. **OWNER-DECIDED 2026-08-14 (`/relay human .`): build BOTH gates — the pre-commit hook AND `relay-doctor`'s install-check promoted to `--strict` on the integrate path.** Rationale for taking both rather than one: each single option has a blind spot the other covers — a commit-time gate cannot see whether OTHER machines re-installed, while a `--strict` relay-doctor only fires when a relay runs and so misses a manifest edit made in a supervised session. Together they catch the drift at authoring time AND at consume time. The **systemd timer was REJECTED**: it is the only option that needs a new reporting channel, and "a log nobody reads" is the id:4347 anti-pattern this very item is filed under — adding a third detector with a weaker channel would reproduce the failure rather than fix it. Implementation split: the pre-commit half belongs in the shared git-hook framework (`id:7a05`/`id:077d`, reconcile-before-greenfield — do NOT author a fourth free-standing hook), triggering on staged changes to a Makefile `*_FILES` list; the relay-doctor half is independent and available now. Both invoke the EXISTING `relay/scripts/check-install-drift.sh` — no new detector. <!-- gated-on:7a05 --> — **PARTIAL 2026-08-21 (`a430f86`): a THIRD invocation site landed, WARN-ONLY.** Front-door step 0c now runs `check-install-drift.sh` at pool launch and surfaces drift loudly but LAUNCHES ANYWAY (owner call: a false positive must not silently kill an unattended run; promote to a refusal only after clean runs). This is an explicit AMENDMENT on new evidence — the 2026-08-21 failure was at LAUNCH, which neither decided gate covers — not a reinterpretation. **BOTH DECIDED GATES REMAIN UNBUILT:** the pre-commit half (still `gated-on:7a05`) and `relay-doctor --strict` on the integrate path (ungated, available now). Third recurrence, and the FIRST to silently break a live run: `integrate.sh` + `ledger-slice.sh` were committed that morning and never installed, so both 404'd on `model:"bash"` — zero dispatch for two rounds, and the merge-to-main path unreachable. <!-- id:83c3 -->

- [ ] [ROUTINE] **`relay-reconcile.sh:209` recommends `--discard` for a STRANDED branch, but `--discard` accepts only PARKED refs — the disposition is reachable, just not by the route the comment names.** `--discard`/`--integrate` resolve their argument under `ORPHAN_NS="relay/orphan/"` (`:91`; documented `:44`/`:47` as "one **parked** branch"), so `--discard relay/<run>-review-repo-0` fails with `no such parked branch 'relay/orphan/relay/<run>-review-repo-0'` — the namespace is prefixed onto a name that already carries its own. **⚠ CORRECTED 2026-08-13 — the first version of this item overstated the defect** by claiming the tool "cannot perform" the disposition and that plain `git branch -D` was required. It is not: **`worktree-retire.sh <repo> <worktree-dir> <branch>` is the sanctioned path** — it removes the worktree force-free, then, finding the branch unmerged, PARKS it as `relay/orphan/<bn>` keeping the ref (`id:a4e9`: refs ARE the registry, never `-D`) — after which `--discard` applies and correctly demands `RELAY_DISCARD_CONFIRM=1`. Verified end-to-end on `relay/relay-20260812-122721-23819-review-repo-0`. So the capability exists and its guardrails are sound; **the defect is documentation coherence.** Three statements in one file disagree: `:209` says `--discard` is the recommended disposition for STRANDED (true only after a retire step it does not mention), the `list` footer says such a branch is "NOT auto-disposable here; inspect, then salvage or park" (accurate), and `:44`/`:47` scope the flags to parked branches (accurate). A reader following `:209` alone hits a confusing error naming a doubly-prefixed ref. Fix: make `:209` name the actual two-step (retire → park → `--discard`), and make the `list` footer say the same, OR add `--park BRANCH` so one flag does the rename and the existing `--discard` follows. Prefer whichever keeps ONE disposal path. **Note the `:209` claim propagated before it was run** — into `f0fdeb1`'s commit message and a `REVIEW_ME.md` note, both asserting `--discard` was the available next step. A claim about code behaviour restated without executing it, which is the CLAUDE.md rule this repo keeps re-learning; the correction above is the same rule applied to my own finding. <!-- id:331a -->

- [ ] [ROUTINE] **A worktree whose branch is MERGED is invisible to every reconcile surface, so merged debris accumulates unreported.** `relay-reconcile.sh` reports parked orphans (`relay/orphan/*`) and, since `id:2b4b`, STRANDED unmerged branches. A worktree whose branch is fully merged is neither, so it is reported by nothing — `relay-reconcile.sh <repo>` printed **"no parked orphans"** and an empty stranded section on 2026-08-13 while **three** worktrees from the 2026-08-12 run sat on disk (`relay-20260812-122721-23819-hard-repo-{0,1,2}` under `~/.cache/relay/worktrees/dotclaude-skills/`), each merged into main, clean, zero unmerged commits — i.e. pure debris with no surface. A fourth (`review-repo-0`) was visible only because its branch happened to be UNMERGED. **This is exactly `id:373e`'s founding motivation recurring**: *"worktrees never got removed and orphan debris accumulated every run"* — `worktree-retire.sh` was built to fix the removal, but nothing DETECTS the case where removal was skipped and the branch then merged. Retired by hand 2026-08-13 (all four; `worktree-retire.sh` handled each force-free — three `git branch -d` clean deletes, one park-then-discard). **The asymmetry to fix**: unmerged leftovers are loud (STRANDED), merged leftovers are silent, yet the merged case is the MORE common one, since a successful integrate is the normal outcome. Contract: a reconcile/doctor pass enumerates `git worktree list` for the repo and reports any relay worktree whose branch is merged as retirable, so the count cannot silently grow; disposal stays human-invoked per `id:a4e9`. Note `git worktree list` is the authority here, not the branch namespace — which is the same lesson as `id:2b4b` (enumerate the thing itself, not a namespace you assume it lives in). <!-- id:8132 -->
- [ ] 🔴 [ROUTINE] **`orphan-scan.sh --shipped` reported TICK-READY for an item that is RED, GATED, and whose ticking would BREAK the suite — the owner-linked-test lookup is unanchored and then silently discards the real owner.** Found 2026-08-26 by a verification pass over the full advisory list; **verified independently, every claim.** **The mechanism**, `meeting/orphan-scan.sh:424`: it resolves an item's test with `grep -rlE "# roadmap:$token([^0-9a-f]|$)" … | head -1`. That pattern is NOT anchored to a file HEADER, so an **inline trailing comment** in an unrelated test claims ownership — and `head -1` then throws away the genuine owner. **Measured on id 6217:** two files match `# roadmap:6217`. The one it picked, `tests/test_make_test_files.sh`, is headed `# roadmap:d3f8` and matches only at line 14, a trailing `# roadmap:6217, currently open+RED` on a fixture-path assignment. It ran that file, saw green, and reported the item TICK-READY. The REAL spec, `tests/test_dryround_single_definition_6217.sh` (properly headed `# roadmap:6217` on line 2), is **RED**: `isDryRound` is still defined twice — `relay/scripts/drain.mjs:102` and `relay/scripts/relay-loop.js:1593`. **Why this is 🔴 and not noise: acting on the advisory would have broken the suite.** `tests/test_make_test_files.sh:18-19` greps ROADMAP.md for that id still being an OPEN checkbox and exits 1 with *"fixture precondition failed: id 6217 is no longer an open ROADMAP item"* — that test **requires it to stay unticked**, because it uses it as its known-RED fixture. So the detector recommended an action that breaks the very file it consulted. The advisory also claimed "no gate": false — `ROADMAP.md:1458` carries `[INPUT — decision]` + `🚧 GATED (auto, id:3801; route:decision-gate)` with two unresolved blockers. **Fix:** anchor the ownership lookup to a header (first ~3 lines), and when several files match, either surface ALL of them or refuse rather than `head -1` — a silent pick among candidates is what turned a RED item green. Same family as the banked "grep the ASSERTIONS, not the filename" lesson, one level up: here it grepped the right token in the wrong file. Relates id:b3ee, id:259f, id:e1bb. <!-- id:535d -->
- [ ] [ROUTINE] **`orphan-scan.sh --shipped`'s GATE-STALE class has ZERO demonstrated signal — 7 of 7 hits were false positives on a full 2026-08-26 sweep.** The rule matches `\b(REMAIN|pending|activation)\b` minus an EXTERNAL-WAIT word, **with no requirement that the word sit in a gating clause at all** — so it fires on the vocabulary rather than on the structure. The seven, each checked: `1cb8` matched a **directory name** (`pending/`, a systemd PathModified target); `9ddd` matched ordinary English (*"surfaces remain singletons"*); `945e` matched a literal `stopReason` **string value** (`blocked-pending-human`); `b3a3` matched a proposed **bucket name** (`pending dispatch`); `55e1` matched an item in a list of *what a handoff doc records*; `c4b4` matched the **bug symptom being described** (*"reported it as pending human input"*). **The seventh is the nastiest shape and is worth the fix on its own: `2895`'s only match is inside the sentence that DISCHARGES the gate** — *"Blocker cleared 2026-07-01 … no longer 'pending shard-prompt work'"*. Writing the discharge **re-arms the alarm, permanently**: the more carefully an author records that a gate is cleared, the louder and more often the detector nags about it. That is an actively perverse incentive, not just noise. **Directions:** (a) require the match to sit in a gating STRUCTURE (a `gated-on:` edge, a `🚧` marker, or a clause-initial "Blocked on/until") rather than anywhere in a 1000-char line; (b) exclude negated/discharged contexts (`no longer`, `cleared`, `NOT gated`) — this is the same anchoring lesson as `id:221f`(b) and `id:259f`, a third instance of the same root; (c) if neither is cheap, **retire the class** — a detector with no true positives in 7 trains readers to ignore the whole report, which costs the classes that DO work. Note the sibling UNMARKED-GATE class is NOT in this state: its regex is tight and it produced real findings, though ~35 of its 55 hits are also FPs, mostly items whose SUBJECT is gate-parsing code and which therefore quote the vocabulary they exist to fix (`5ed7`/`b724`/`e7af` are literally the items filed to fix unanchored gate matching — and the detector trips on them). The tail is genuinely cheap — 338 files under 0.5s CPU totalling 50.4s. **One mechanism dominates**: 82 of 439 tests (19%) invoke the `relay-doctor → classify-repo → unpromoted-scan` chain and account for **161.2s of 262.4s CPU (61%)**. **Ranked, with MEASURED wins.** **P1 — parallelise `run-tests.sh`: 3.1-3.6x, measured.** It is strictly sequential today (a plain `for` loop at `tests/run-tests.sh:48-66`; a grep for `&`/`xargs`/`-P`/`wait` returns nothing). 147-file subset 49.3s → 13.8s; 156-file subset incl. heavy files 140.1s → 44.6s with 155/156 identical results; contention overhead only +9% CPU. Prototype in scratchpad `prof/run-parallel.sh`, preserving EXPECTED-RED semantics. **No genuinely parallel-unsafe test was found** — but that is verified for 156 of 439 files, NOT all, and the static scan for fixed `/tmp` paths and lock filenames was too noisy to report as clean; a full `-P8` run against a sequential baseline would settle the remaining 283. **P2 — make `test_chain_end_reask_mechanical.sh` hermetic: ~35s CPU (13% of the suite), ESTIMATE.** It is the single most expensive file at 40.0s CPU because lines 52 and 66 drive `classify-repo.sh` against the LIVE repo (`id:a245`). Not implemented because it changes what the test drives, which touches assertions. Its cost GROWS with the ledger. **P3 — optimise `unpromoted-scan.sh`: 8.1x, measured** — see `id:0ccf`; projected suite saving 60-80s CPU (25-30%), which is an EXTRAPOLATION, not an observation. **Do P2/P3 before P1**: the 40s file is the Amdahl floor bounding any width. **Not worth doing**: fork reduction elsewhere (476 forks = 0.3s), git fixture setup (65 `git init`s, all into `mktemp -d`), and sleeps. **Sleep census: no padding exists** — 15 call sites, ~15.5s actually blocking (5%), every one waiting on a real async condition (heartbeat TTLs, flock acquisition, timeout nets); the rest are never waited on. **Network egress: NONE** — all `curl`/`wget`/`nc` hits are source-greps of script text. **The original urgency argument PARTLY SURVIVES**: agents did abandon full runs and substitute hand-curated subsets, one of which omitted the two primary tests of the file it had just modified and reported green over red. But the cause was external load, not inherent suite slowness — the honest lesson is "check what else is on the box before trusting or blaming a timing", not "the suite is too slow to run". <!-- id:5785 -->

- [ ] [ROUTINE] **`tests/test_git_lock_push_slash_branch.sh` is LOAD-FLAKY, and its own intermittency instrumentation does not fire when it fails.** Observed 2026-08-14: PASSED in one full-suite run, FAILED in a later loaded run with `push did not reach remote on slash-named branch`, PASSES in isolation. Cause not conclusively established; the load hypothesis is supported from the code itself: `git-diary-workflow/git-lock-push.sh` wraps `git push` in a hard `timeout` (tunable via `GIT_LOCK_PUSH_TIMEOUT`) whose documented behaviour is "on timeout: warn loud, release the flock, exit 0 — work stays committed", i.e. **a SKIP that returns SUCCESS to the caller**, and the test's own line-56 comment already says "intermittent failure we need to see WHICH skip path fired (flock timeout, ...)". **The actionable half is the instrumentation gap**: the author anticipated this exact intermittency and instrumented for it, yet the recorded failure emitted ONLY the assertion, with no skip-path line — the one artefact that would distinguish flock-timeout from push-timeout from a real regression was missing at the moment it was needed. **Fix the diagnostic emission FIRST; do NOT simply raise the timeout**, which would hide which path fired and destroy the information already identified as necessary. Same silent-fallback shape as `id:729c` (a write path that echoed a token receipt without writing) and `id:0ccf`. <!-- id:24fa -->

- [ ] [ROUTINE] [INBOUND routed:ca0f from loderite] **OWNER ASK 2026-08-14 — relay worktree creation does a FULL `npm install` per worktree; use btrfs reflink CoW instead.** MEASURED by the filer, not assumed: loderite's `node_modules` is 226 MB / 285 packages, and the repo copy plus one live worktree copy total **449 MB under a single `du`** — i.e. ZERO hardlink sharing, npm made a genuine full copy. Alternative measured on this host: `cp -a --reflink=always node_modules <worktree>/` completed in **1 second** with `btrfs filesystem du -s` reporting **Exclusive: 0.00 B** (146 MiB set-shared) — a 226 MB tree for zero new space, versus a full install. **INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED HERE 2026-08-14**: `~/src` is btrfs (`/dev/nvme0n1p2[/@home]`), and `~/.cache/relay/worktrees` is **1.8 GB**. **REFLINK, NOT A SYMLINK — and the discriminator is correctness, not speed.** The owner floated both; they are not equivalent. A shared or symlinked `node_modules` is MUTABLE SHARED STATE (vite/vitest write `node_modules/.vite`; npm/postinstall scripts write in-tree), so two concurrent worktrees — the normal relay case, `POOL_WIDTH` defaults to 5 — would race and corrupt each other. Reflink copies cheaply and diverges on first write, so it is concurrency-safe by construction. **SCOPE**: the worktree-creation path (SKILL.md invariant 4's `git worktree add`) should, when the source repo has a `node_modules` and the FS supports CoW, reflink it into the new worktree and otherwise fall back to today's behaviour — `cp --reflink=auto` degrades to a normal copy on non-CoW filesystems, so a probe is only needed to decide whether to skip entirely. Node-only; irrelevant to python/uv repos. **STALE DOC TO FIX ALONGSIDE**: the relay's worktree guidance repeats the claim that `node_modules` is "npm-cache-backed, so mostly fast linking — inherent to worktrees and fine". Measured: it is not linking at all, and not fine. Textbook constraint-archaeology — an assertion that was never measured. **COUNT CORRECTION, verified here**: the filing reports "13 worktree dirs live on disk"; `find ~/.cache/relay/worktrees -maxdepth 1 -type d` returns **61** (0 non-directory entries). So the reap backlog is substantially worse than filed — abandoned worktrees from 2026-07-24/26/31 and 2026-08-12 are named in the source item, but the total is 61, not 13. The reap path needs its own look; do not size that work off the filed number. **GENERALISED 2026-08-14 on owner input — this is NOT an npm-specific item.** The owner notes the same symlink-vs-reflink question applies to the Lean build trees in `lodelore`, `mathematical-writing` and `toesnail`. So the unit of work is the relay worktree-creation path handling **large regenerable artifact trees generically**, not `node_modules` as a special case: at minimum `node_modules` (npm) and `.lake` (Lean), with `.venv`, Rust `target/` and similar as candidates. **The correctness discriminator carries over unchanged and is arguably STRONGER for Lean**: a symlinked or shared tree is mutable shared state, and `lake` writes into `.lake/build` continuously during a build, so two concurrent worktrees at the default `POOL_WIDTH` of 5 would race — whereas reflink copies cheaply and diverges on first write. **PER-ECOSYSTEM VERIFICATION IS REQUIRED, NOT ASSUMED**: the 226 MB / 1 s / `Exclusive: 0.00 B` figures were measured for one npm tree on this host; the equivalent numbers for a `.lake` tree, and whether anything in it is host-absolute or otherwise unsafe to copy, must be measured per ecosystem before extending the mechanism to it. Do not generalise the MEASUREMENT along with the design. **Also check for the same unmeasured "it is fine" assertion** in those repos' own docs — loderite carried one for `node_modules` ("npm-cache-backed, so mostly fast linking") that measurement refuted; a Lean-side equivalent is likely and would be the same constraint-archaeology failure. <!-- routed:ca0f --> <!-- id:3a6c -->

- [ ] [HARD] **PROPOSAL, owner's call — mechanize the "same fact computed twice in one round" detector.** Three defects filed independently on 2026-08-14 by two different repos share one shape: a dispatch-path script re-derives state that a shared, tested primitive ALREADY resolved in the same round, and discards the primitive's answer. Instances: `id:7517` (the HARD-child brief re-grepped the pool-lane list instead of consuming `gather-repo-state`'s resolved one, using the retired spelling, and refused 5 real items); `id:ec2c` (`roadmap-lint.sh:414` emits DECOMPOSED-CONTAINER and NOTHING invokes it — zero call sites across the five dispatch scripts); `id:d167` (`unpromoted-scan.sh` re-derives gate state without `lib-typed-edges.sh`, which `gather-repo-state.sh` already consumes). **The sharpening that makes it mechanizable** (credit: the loderite session): "a shared primitive exists somewhere" is unfalsifiable and un-lintable, but **"the same fact computed twice in one round by two different methods, one result discarded"** is a detectable signature — `gather` computed `open_hard_pool` while the child re-grepped it; `roadmap-lint` computed the container verdict while dispatch never read it. That turns a code-review sensibility into a lint, which is the form the global mechanize-first heuristic asks for. **NEGATIVE RESULT, recorded so the class is not padded**: loderite's follow-up executor audit explicitly returned NO fourth instance (`gaming-scan.sh` behaved correctly; the pattern did not appear). The class stands at three, not "growing". **ADJACENT SHAPE, same family, opposite direction** (loderite `id:9c94`): building a primitive NOBODY calls — the gate you cannot trip; three items there had hardened a guard with no production consumer. Naming both directions together is what makes this more than an anecdote. **NOT DECIDED — this is a proposal carrying a peer session's evidence and sharpening, not a ratified conclusion.** — **COUNT REVERTED 2026-08-18 (meeting `docs/meeting-notes/2026-08-18-1052-meeting-backlog-selector-948c-788f.md`, D3b): the class stays at THREE.** Earlier that same session the resolve-gates-vs-roadmap-lint gate disagreement was ratified as a FOURTH instance; the `--fabled` closing pass refuted it and the owner reverted. It fails this item's own signature — "the same fact computed twice **in one round** by two different methods, **one result discarded**" — on all three qualifiers: **(a) not the same fact** (`roadmap-lint.sh:348-354` documents a deliberate different-question split; only the archive-ticked subcase overlaps); **(b) nothing is discarded** (both outputs are emitted AND consumed — `classify-repo.sh:36,107` consumes resolve-gates, roadmap-lint runs on the doctor/handoff/human paths); **(c) not one round** (different drivers, different invocation contexts). It is instead "two persistent implementations of one predicate drifting" — filed under `id:8de9`, which already names it. Note the widened reading is not even self-consistent at n=4: `id:ca9e`'s edit-integrity note from the same morning would be a fifth. **This is the recorded negative result working as intended** — the item forbids widening twice, and the count was padded within hours of that being written. <!-- id:7877 --> — **DECIDED 2026-08-18 (`/relay human .`, OWNER: BUILD IT). Re-laned `[INPUT — decision]` → `[HARD]`** (pool-executable apex work; the lint's signature needs judgement to specify, so it is not cheap-tier `[ROUTINE]`). Build the detector for the signature as sharpened: **the same fact computed twice in one round by two different methods, one result discarded** — that is the falsifiable, lintable form, unlike "a shared primitive exists somewhere". **Scope is the ONE direction decided here**: the three named instances (`id:7517`, `id:ec2c`, `id:d167`) are the seed fixtures. **The adjacent opposite direction — a primitive nobody calls, loderite `id:9c94` — was OFFERED as a combined build and NOT chosen**; do not silently widen into it. Note the class stands at **three, not growing**: loderite's follow-up executor audit returned NO fourth instance (`gaming-scan.sh` behaved correctly), and that negative result is recorded here so the build is not justified by a padded count. Contract: a fixture dispatch-path script that re-derives a fact `gather-repo-state.sh` already resolved in the same round produces a LOUD finding naming both computation sites and which result was discarded; a script that consumes the primitive's answer exits 0 and prints nothing. **AMENDED 2026-08-18 (`/relay human .`, action item 3 of meeting `2026-08-18-1052`, D3b REVERTED): the class stays at n=3 — the n=4 recorded earlier that session is WITHDRAWN.** The roadmap-lint/resolve-gates disagreement was counted as a fourth instance; it fails this item's own ratified signature (*the same fact computed twice IN ONE ROUND by two different methods, ONE result DISCARDED*) on all three qualifiers: **not the same fact** (the code comment documents a deliberate different-question split), **nothing discarded** (both outputs are emitted and consumed — `classify-repo.sh:36,107` consumes resolve-gates, while roadmap-lint runs on the doctor/handoff/human paths), and **not one round** (different drivers, different invocation contexts). This item's own text forbids widening the signature twice, and the widened reading is not self-consistent at n=4 — `id:ca9e`'s edit-integrity note from the same morning would then be a fifth. The disagreement files under `id:8de9` instead, which already names *two implementations of one predicate* as the drift that caused it. Recorded so it is not re-counted.

- [ ] [ROUTINE] **`review.md` §2b.1 defines the RESURRECTION CHECK but never states its LIMIT** (INBOUND from loderite, `docs/meeting-notes/2026-08-14-1338-empty-dispatch-container-and-vocab.md`) — the check (run the ORIGINAL specs against the NEW implementation) proves only that rejections **pinned by the original assertions** survived; a widening can flip an entirely UNPINNED rejection class and still return a clean 30/30. That is what happened on loderite `id:89ef`: the resurrection run was 30/30 green and honest, and the sentence written about it — *"zero rejections flipped to acceptances, the widening is strictly additive"* — was false, because the old code rejected permuted-order region pairs via an index-by-index comparison that no test asserted. **The check ran, the check was honest, and the SENTENCE ABOUT THE CHECK over-claimed** — no amount of re-running would have caught it; this is the claim-about-code-is-a-derived-doc rule in its subtlest form. **Suggested addition to §2b.1** (phrasing from the gate-C reviewer, quoted verbatim): *"A green resurrection run bounds the widening only over behaviour the original spec asserted. Before claiming 'strictly additive', separately enumerate the rejection classes the old implementation produced that no test pinned, and probe those directly."* **Fold in the earlier caveat on the same technique in the SAME revision**: a green run is not a pass/fail gate — legitimate contract tightenings produce expected reds, and the only finding is a rejection→acceptance flip. Deliverable: a ranked list, each row = meeting item · count and ids of what it blocks · whether any blocked item is itself queued/dispatchable. Items blocking nothing are PARKED OPENLY (stated as parked, not silently deprioritised) — not closed, not aged out; the owner explicitly did NOT choose the age-out sweep. **RUN THE RESULT UNDER A `--fabled` ADVERSARIAL PASS before treating the ranking as settled** (owner directive, same answer) — the `--fabled` escalation trigger has fired four times, every time on a rationale whose factual premise did not survive checking, and a blocking-graph ranking is exactly the shape that rots: it rests on edge markers being complete and correctly targeted, which this session already found untrue twice (`id:2b49`'s gate reads DEAD but is SATISFIED via the archive; `id:a955`/`id:3ca7` were gated on the rule rather than the ranking). **Cross-check the edges before trusting the rank** — a missing `gated-on:` marker makes a load-bearing item look like it blocks nothing, which is the failure mode that would make this triage actively harmful. invoke the scanner at BUILD time. **AMENDED 2026-08-18 (`/relay human .`, action item 1 of meeting `docs/meeting-notes/2026-08-18-1052-meeting-backlog-selector-948c-788f.md`).** The consumption clause directing the implementer to consume `resolve-gates.sh` and *never re-derive the edge set by grep* is WRONG FOR THIS ARTIFACT and must not be obeyed literally. **Verified in code 2026-08-18:** `resolve-gates.sh` builds its satisfaction state map over FOUR ledgers (`typed_edges_build_state_map` over ROADMAP.md + TODO.md + TODO.archive.md + ROADMAP.archive.md, `:44-45`) — but the loop that EMITS rows is fed `done < "$roadmap"` (`:70`), i.e. it enumerates edge-carrying lines from **ROADMAP.md alone**, and emits nothing at all for a satisfied edge. ⚠ Cite `:70` for this, NOT the `:45-49` span the meeting note used — `:45` IS the four-ledger state map, so quoting it as the ROADMAP-only evidence points at the one line that proves the opposite. **Consequence:** an implementer obeying the clause builds the reverse blocking graph from ROADMAP-resident edges only, with zero satisfied-edge data — making D1b's distinction (blocks-nothing-because-resolved vs blocks-nothing-because-nothing-depends-on-it) unsatisfiable by construction. **Consume instead:** `lib-typed-edges.sh`'s extractors + `typed_edges_build_state_map` over the four-ledger span;
